newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to protect pay-TV, on-line services from piracy.
newsitem.headline: EU to protect pay-TV, on-line services from piracy.

text.p: The European Commission, seeking to boost a key growth industry, proposed legislation on Wednesday to protect expanding services such as pay-TV and electronic publishing from piracy.
The planned European Union law would strengthen legal protection of television, radio broadcasting and information society services which consumers must pay to access.

It would require EU member states to "prohibit and provide appropriate sanctions against all commercial activities related to unauthorised access to a protected service, such as the sale of pirate decoders, smart cards or software," the Commission said in a statement.

According to industry estimates, suppliers of these services lose more than five percent of total turnover because of commercial pirate equipment, such as decoders enabling viewers to watch television programmes without paying the operator.

"This directive aims at rendering illegal pirate equipment...this is going after the commercial companies which generate enormous benefits on the backs of other people," a Commission official told reporters.
Because of piracy equipment, many of these services faced "serious problems which hampers their economic development," she added. Current rules did not provide sufficient protection.
EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti said the plan would help electronic commerce, a sector set to grow rapidly as more and more people get connected to the Internet.
Protection from piracy for services based on so-called conditional access, including also video-on-demand and a wide range of on-line services, was essential, he said.

"Without pan-European Union protection, service providers will be reluctant to invest in conditional access services, which are one of most promising areas of industrial growth," Monti said in a statement.

The proposed legislation, which needs to be approved by EU ministers as well as by the European Parliament, was not aimed at the consumer of such services, nor at the "teenage hacker," the Commission official said. "The root of the problem is the commercial piracy industry," she added.

Currently, there is a patchwork of different national rules with some member states having introduced protection against piracy while for example Germany and Denmark have no specific legislation at all.
This distorts competition and creates problems for the single market in the 15-nation bloc, the official said.
"There is a need to introduce harmonised protection at the European level, which will create a level playing field."
But she also stressed that it was a global problem, referring to a hugely popular site on the world wide web set up in October which advocates and promotes pirate equipment.

"This demonstrates the new marketing possibilities which are increasingly occurring at the global level," she said. "We need to aim at international protection and the Commission is considering now how this can be achieved."
No other country outside the EU offered the same kind of protection which the Commission is now proposing, she said.
